These results show that the rate-\(1/2\) regime of qLDPC codes can be extended from reconfigurable platforms to superconducting hardware, providing a route toward low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum processors.

items.title: Integrated GPU Core for Mamba-3
items.summary:
Mamba-3, the latest Mamba state-space model (SSM), enables efficient long-context modeling, matching Mamba-2 perplexity with half the state size and increasing decoding arithmetic intensity. However, its multi-input multi-output (MIMO) computation, exponential-trapezoidal discretization, and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) introduce dense, element-wise, and sequential operations. Despite kernel fusion, conventional GPUs execute these operations inefficiently.

Our characterization of Mamba-3 hybrid models reveals numerous kernel launches, substantial data movement, and increased register pressure that reduces warp occupancy and memory-latency hiding. We propose RescuCore, a specialized GPU execution unit for Mamba-3 inference that retains other hybrid model layers on existing GPU resources. Integrated alongside CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores within each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) sub-partition, RescuCore shares the register file, shared memory, and warp schedulers.

Dense projections remain on conventional GPU resources, while RescuCore pipelines discretization, normalization, RoPE, MIMO computation, recurrent state updates, and output gating to reduce kernel fragmentation and intermediate data movement. We select BF16 after evaluating multiple numerical formats, preserving model accuracy with an estimated area overhead of 5.9% of an A100 die for state size 32 and MIMO rank 4. We evaluate RescuCore using cycle-accurate Accel-Sim simulation, RTL synthesis, and synthesis-informed AccelWattch power modeling.

Compared with conventional GPU execution, RescuCore achieves 1.4-9.4x speedup and 1.4-5.0x energy reduction during prefill, and 1.3-2.8x speedup and 1.2-2.6x energy reduction during autoregressive decoding. These results demonstrate the potential of GPU-integrated specialized execution for SSM-based hybrid models.

items.title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
items.summary:
GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution.

Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement.

Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone.

Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.

items.title: Benchmarking LLM Inference on Desktop-Scale NVIDIA Grace Blackwell Clusters
items.summary:
Two NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems connect directly over 200 GbE to serve larger language models and increase inference capacity, but the benefits depend on how they are deployed. We benchmark 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, 8B to 235B parameters and four weight precisions on one and two RDMA-connected systems. Using vLLM, we compare tensor parallelism (TP=2), pipeline parallelism (PP=2) and a two-replica baseline at concurrency 1 to 64, with three independent launches per configuration.

TP=2 delivers a median 1.59x peak-throughput gain over one Spark, versus 1.39x for PP=2 and has higher throughput in 93 of 96 matched comparisons with separated 95% Welch intervals. It reduces unloaded inter-token latency to 0.52x to 0.73x of one Spark, whereas PP=2 provides little reduction. TP=2 also achieves the highest goodput under a strict 100 ms inter-token latency objective wherever both strategies are supported and the objective is met.

For models fitting on one Spark, TP=2 generally favors low-concurrency serving, while replication offers higher throughput at high concurrency. One Spark uses less GPU energy per output token at matched concurrency. Across three precision ladders, NVFP4 reduces unloaded latency more than adding a second Spark at BF16.

NCCL microbenchmarks and comparisons with an earlier TCP campaign suggest that collective communication overhead contributes to the advantage of TP=2. These results provide deployment guidance for desktop-scale inference.

items.title: CECAR: Cache & Expert Co-Aware Routing Accelerates On-Device Inference of MoE LLMs
items.summary:
Despite growing interest in on-device LLM deployment, large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remain impractical on resource-constrained devices, as sparse expert activation still requires all expert weights to be memory-resident. To address this, we identify three key observations for on-device MoE inference: (a) cache hit rates are fundamentally bounded even under Belady's optimal policy; (b) these bounds are insufficient for low-latency on-device inference; and (c) prior cache-aware routing based on binary cache presence can induce routing instability.

Based on these insights, we propose CECAR (Cache & Expert Co-Aware Routing), a MoE inference system that jointly considers expert routing and cache management. Unlike prior cache-aware routing methods, CECAR uses an ML-based cache policy to predict the expected reuse distance of each expert and prioritizes routing and execution toward experts with smaller predicted reuse distances.

On the Qwen3-30B-A3B model, CECAR achieves 12.5 tokens/s on a consumer-grade GPU with only 16 GB of VRAM, where non-resident experts are fetched from SSD, delivering a 4.5x speedup over conventional MoE inference and exceeding the decode speed of baselines that keep the entire model fully resident in DRAM. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/CECAR.

items.title: High-Throughput Serving of Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe with Regime-Aware Megakernels and Kernel Fusion
items.summary:
Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR leaderboards. Serving it efficiently takes more than fast operators: continuous batching changes the amount and mix of work at every iteration, and the best fusion granularity changes with it.

We present a serving engine that, for every pass, chooses between persistent megakernels and chains of fused kernels at crossovers measured offline. On an H100 SXM GPU, throughput of our accuracy-preserving serving peaks at 4,345x real time, 1.39x the peak of tuned vLLM, and is up to 4.39x faster at low concurrency; on B200 it peaks at 6,367x, 1.64x vLLM at the highest concurrency we measured.

Word error rate (WER) is 1.91 to 1.93% against 1.88 to 1.93% for vLLM. Within a 400 ms budget for p95 end-to-end completion time, it serves 8x as many concurrent requests.

Choosing per pass beats either level alone: 23% higher throughput than always using megakernels at 128 concurrent requests, and 9% higher than always using fused kernels at 8. Opt-in switches, including greedy MoE layer skipping, add 13 to 16% throughput on B200 for offline jobs that can accept higher WER.

items.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
items.summary:
This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.

Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.

Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my LLM gallery .

But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.

Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover

different positional methods in LLMs;

(finally) how RoPE works;

items.title: Multi-Branch Transformer
items.summary:
Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers.

At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases.

To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss.

These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.

items.title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
items.summary:
Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency.

Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree.

Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution.

Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.

items.title: From Facts to Personas: Interpretable Role Unlearning in LLMs via Mixture-of-Experts
items.summary:
LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs.

To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained.

We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces.

This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles.

All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.

items.title: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
items.summary:
Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead.

To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR).

These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length.

Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

items.title: Empowering Masked Diffusion Models to Self-Correct with Leave-One-Out Transformers
items.summary:
Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for language modeling, enabling parallel token generation with competitive performance. Yet standard MDMs suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) inability to revise tokens, and (2) sparse training signal.

We revisit hollow transformers, which address both limitations by predicting each token from its surrounding context, independently of the input at that position. We introduce the Leave-One-Out Transformer (LOOT), a more efficient and expressive architecture that advances hollow transformers through two complementary advances.

First, we redesign the merging mechanism to enable frequent interaction between left and right contexts, substantially improving predictive performance over prior hollow transformers. Second, we derive a lower-variance estimator of the MDM NELBO that supervises all tokens and improves validation perplexity.

Together, these advances yield a competitive standalone diffusion language model capable of effective self-correction during inference. On LM1B, LOOT matches the strongest dense-supervision MDM baseline in validation perplexity.

On OpenWebText, LOOT achieves higher MAUVE and better generation quality-diversity tradeoffs than prior remasking methods, using $8\times$ fewer forward evaluations and $3.5\times$ fewer inference FLOPs.

items.title: Bilateral Log-Linear Attention
items.summary:
Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall.

Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin.

By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds.

For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

items.title: SpecRelay: Amortize or Avoid the Round Trip in Edge-Cloud Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows.

To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule).

At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks.

At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.

items.title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
items.summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute.

On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training.

We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead.

We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs.

On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.

items.title: On the pure part of the cohomology of character varieties
items.summary:
We prove the purity conjecture of Hausel and Rodriguez-Villegas relating the graded dimension of the pure part of the cohomology of the twisted character variety $M^B(r,d)$ of $GL(r)$ of genus $g$ with the cohomology of a suitable quiver variety associated to the quiver $S_g$ with one vertex and $g$ loops.

In particular, this provides an explicit formula for the pure part of the mixed Hodge polynomial of $M^B(r,d)$ in terms of the Kac polynomial $A_{S_g,r}(q)$.

Our approach is based on the $P=W$ theorem to transfer the purity conjecture into a statement about the perverse filtration on the cohomology of th stack of Higgs bundles on a genus $g$ curve.

We use the theory of BPS Lie algebras, their $χ$-independence property (proven by Kinjo-Koseki), the recent proof of the stack version of $P=C$ due to Picovschi and Davison's analytic neighborhood theorem to reduce the conjecture to a comparison problem between (the 'pure' part) of the BPS Lie algebra asociated to the stack of Higgs bundles on a genus $g$ curve and the BPS Lie algebra of the stack of representations of the preprojective algebra of the quiver $S_g$.

This last step is taken care of by a quiver analog of Markman's tautological generation theorem for the BPS Lie algebra of arbitrary quivers (this last result is also proven by Davison and Hennecart).

items.title: Atom Computing Finalizes $100 Million U.S. Department of Commerce R&D Award
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Atom Computing signed an agreement for up to $100 million with the U.S. Department of Commerce to accelerate development of fault-tolerant, utility-scale quantum computers.

The funding will support in-house technology development, expanded engineering and testing infrastructure, and collaboration with supply chain partners.

Atom Computing also advanced to Stage C of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, with potential funding of up to $300 million.

PRESS RELEASE — Atom Computing , a leader in scalable neutral-atom quantum computing, today announced it has signed an agreement for up to $100 million with the U.S. Department of Commerc e to accelerate research and development of fault-tolerant, utility-scale quantum computers. The award follows a Letter of Intent announced earlier this year and represents a significant investment in advancing next-generation computing technologies critical to U.S. economic competitiveness, scientific leadership, and national security.

Atom Computing ‘s neutral-atom architecture is increasingly recognized as one of the most viable approaches for building large-scale, commercially useful quantum computers. Today’s announcement closely follows the company’s recent selection as the only neutral atom company to advance to Stage C of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (DARPA QBI) with potential funding up to $300 million.

Atom has consistently demonstrated technical leadership through several industry milestones, including being the first to build a platform with more than 1,000 qubits, the first neutral-atom company to demonstrate sub-threshold behavior on a system with full, end-to-end quantum error correction over many rounds, and the first to commercially offer a logical-qubit quantum computer. In 2025 Atom Computing sold its first commercial on-premises quantum computer to QuNorth, a Nordic quantum initiative funded by EIFO and Novo Nordisk Foundation.

items.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
items.summary:
Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes.

The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc.

Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects.

We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc.

Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.

items.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
items.summary:
Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding.

We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens.

Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted.

We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load.

We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.

items.title: Tessa: Encoding Classical Data Across an Entire Quantum Processor
items.summary:
We present Tessa, a hardware-aware, device-wide scheme to encode classical data on quantum computers. We use it to experimentally encode and decode up to $1568$ real values using IBM's Phoenix and Fez quantum computers on a variety of data.

Tessa's construction is an extension of QPIXL and QCrank. However, it checkerboards address and data qubits across a coupling graph with neighbouring data qubits sharing only a subset of address qubits.

When using the device's coupling graph no SWAP gates or routing is required, but the construction works for any bipartite coupling graph. The shots required for readout are determined by the local coupling degree.

As examples, we have used cat states (pixel art of cats), various pixel art, audio, MIDI, DNA sequences and protein amino acid sequences.

items.title: CoPre-MoE: Consolidating and Preserving MoE for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
items.summary:
Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth.

Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE).

For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool.

We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.

items.title: Observing Enhanced Entanglement in an Ising Quantum Register Beyond Weak Measurement
items.summary:
Measurements often yield a disentangled quantum state which is the most probable measurement outcome while the measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement could be exponentially less probable or absent. Higher probability in measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement is virtue in experimental observation of enhance entanglement in post-selected or Born-rule measurements with less resources in noisy quantum devices.

We develop a periodic measurement sampling(PMS) protocol in the framework of uniform matrix product states. Using PMS, we identify a peak enhancement of entanglement in a uniform post-measurement state whose probabilistic outcome can be maximized by optimizing a measurement super-cell.

A measurement super-cell is the smallest repeating building block of qubits defined by the measurement density, external field strength and exchange interactions between quantum register and ancilla qubits. The above prediction based on a classical description of the many-body quantum state is demonstrated in a quantum computing experiment in a loop of quantum register qubits with Ising interactions in the presence of transverse magnetic field.

Further, we show the scalability of predictions of the periodic measurement sampling protocol in the thermodynamic limit to finite size systems. Especially, we present a rescaling ansatz which would enable predicting the possibility of observing enhanced entanglement in finite size systems.

items.title: Release v5.23.0
items.summary:
Release v5.23.0

New Model additions

Inkling2

Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs, and it is intended for use in English and other languages and across multiple coding languages. Its language backbone has 48 mixture-of-experts decoder layers, each routing tokens to 8 of 384 experts, for 594B total and 17B active parameters. It keeps the Inkling decoder (learned relative attention, short causal convolutions, mixture-of-experts layers) and adds block attention residuals, gated attention with a learned sink, and dynamic key/value convolutions. Images are encoded by a Perception Encoder-based vision transformer and projected into the language model embeddings, one embedding per 40x40 pixel patch.

items.title: Entropic quantum error correction for independent and correlated amplitude damping errors
items.summary:
The idea of using quantum entropy for quantum error correction (QEC) has existed for a long time. However, its computational complexity has limited its practical use: even a $[[4,1]]$ code for standard independent amplitude damping errors involves a $256\times 256$ Hermitian matrix, so the approach scales poorly as the codeword length increases.

For correlated errors, the situation is even worse. In this paper, we show that, by using the insights developed in our previous paper and exploiting certain structures of quantum conditional mutual information, we can solve these problems exactly by hand, using only $2\times 2$ unitary matrices.

By examining the entropy, we identify the leakage channels and the amount of leakage exactly, then define the recovery map accordingly. The rules defining our recovery map are simple, intuitive, and computationally inexpensive: for independent errors, it is based on 16 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions; for correlated errors, it is based on 6 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions.

Our method sacrifices little in terms of performance: for the widely used entanglement fidelity, our simple QEC recovery map achieves a sharp result; for the worst-case fidelity, the best result is about $9\%$ better than ours; for correlated errors, there are no comparable results for short codewords. Among the known techniques, our recovery map is the first non-global one.

The calculations use elementary linear algebra and calculus, and is presented in great detail.

items.title: Quantum phase estimation on a Rydberg quantum simulator
items.summary:
Determining the energy spectrum of a many-body quantum system is a central goal of quantum physics. Ground-state energies underpin materials science and quantum chemistry, whereas excited states govern dynamical phenomena such as quantum thermalization.

Quantum simulators have greatly shaped our understanding of many-body systems, for example, by enabling access to microscopic mechanisms and nonlocal order parameters. However, experiments still struggle to access the full range of many-body spectral features and are typically limited to measuring energy gaps and excitations by spectroscopic means.

Here, we address this challenge by demonstrating quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg quantum simulator. We reconstruct the complex-valued return amplitude, or Loschmidt echo, of an initial probe state.

From its Fourier transform, we measure absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in systems of up to 19 atoms in one and two spatial dimensions. Varying the initial probe state, we select distinct spectral windows within which we compute the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, and observe their competition across the many-body spectrum.

Our results thereby demonstrate phase-sensitive many-body spectroscopy on an analog quantum simulator without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.

items.title: Efficient Iterative Symmetrization algorithm for quantum computing and hadron applications
items.summary:
Efficient algorithms for the (anti)symmetrization of quantum registers are necessary for upcoming few- and many-body physics applications, from atomic to particle-physics scales. We propose a recursive algorithm (anti)symmetrizing the last particle added to memory, each time one is created or destroyed, respect to the rest of already (anti)symmetrized ones.

Given a generalized Dicke state (GDS) of $(j-1)$ quantum registers, each assigned to a particle, the algorithm produces another GDS of $j$ registers (of $n_{qb}$ qubits each) using a mere $\mathcal{O}(j\log_2^2 j + j n_{qb})$ $\mathtt{CNOT}$ and single-qubit gates, and $3j+\lceil\log_2j\rceil+\mathcal{O}(\max(n_{qb},\log_2 j))$ clean auxiliary qubits. The (anti)symmetrizing operator constructed for this purpose depends on the quantum numbers of the additional particle being introduced or ``created''.

The algorithm improves upon the construction presented in Appendix A of \cite{Galvez-Viruet:2024hry} by almost two powers of $j$ and is on par with the most efficient methods to date, while ideally suited for dynamical memory management with variable particle number. We exemplify its applicability with a small selection of problems from hadron physics which are expected to be addressable with upcoming quantum computers.

items.title: Max-Cut QAOA on Non-Hardware-Native Graphs via MinLA Surrogates and Configuration Recovery
items.summary:
For non-hardware-native \textsc{MAX-CUT} instances, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can incur additional two-qubit depth overhead due to SWAP-based routing of interactions between non-adjacent qubits. We propose a hybrid quantum--classical workflow that reduces this depth by selectively removing interactions and subsequently recovers solution quality through classical optimization of the original \textsc{MAX-CUT} objective.

We employ a Minimum Linear Arrangement (MinLA)-based vertex ordering to preferentially retain short-range interactions, thereby constructing a two-qubit depth-reduced surrogate QAOA ansatz. To compensate for the information lost through interaction removal, we develop classical \textit{recovery} strategies that refine QPU-sampled bitstrings directly on the original \textsc{MAX-CUT} objective.

We develop two recovery strategies: signed-residue-based local search and bipartite-block optimization, where each conditional block problem is solved exactly using an $s$--$t$ minimum cut. Recovery is performed independently on each sampled configuration, ensuring monotonic improvement in cut value without additional QPU executions.

We evaluate the workflow on \texttt{ibm\_kingston} for 120 distinct non-hardware-native instances comprising $6$-regular and Erdős--Rényi graphs with 40, 60 and 100 vertices. We verify that the surrogates substantially reduce transpiled two-qubit depth while staying within the prescribed two-qubit depth, and with recovery yield \textit{near-optimal} cuts on the original graphs.

These results demonstrate the potential of hardware-aware interaction selection and classical recovery to extend QAOA to graph instances whose full cost Hamiltonians exceed practical circuit-depth budgets.

items.title: Fuse-All MoE Inference Kernel with Load Balancing on TPUs
items.summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs.

To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip.

Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode.

Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16.

With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.

items.title: The Geometry of Quantum Memory: How Anyons Rewrite the Rules of Remembering and Computation in the Quantum Realm
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Topological quantum computing aims to store quantum information in a system’s global, topological properties. There, local noise cannot reach it, potentially cutting the large qubit overhead that conventional error correction demands.

Anyons are quasiparticles that emerged from the theoretical work of Jon Magne Leinaas and Jan Myrheim (1977), and Frank Wilczek (1982). They gained a physical home in the fractional quantum Hall effect, and Alexei Kitaev tied them to computing in 1997.

Experiments directly observed Abelian anyons in 2020. But, researchers have yet to conclusively observe, in a real material, the non-Abelian anyons needed for computation by braiding. This makes their search one of the field’s most ambitious bets.

An ordinary qubit remembers too much and listens too well. Its delicate phase is the hidden part of a qubit’s state. It carries much of the qubit’s information and is very easy to disturb. The phase takes account of every stray field, lattice vibration, and fluctuating charge. In turn, a qubit lives a fragile existence and decoheres due to unwanted interactions with its environment.

But what if we could curb a qubit’s ability to listen to the environment, giving it a selective “amnesia”? What if a qubit could store information somewhere local disturbances cannot see? And what if its operations depended on how particles are tangled, rather than exactly how they move?

This is the core idea behind topological quantum computation and it all begins with the two-dimensional loophole that brings to life the strange particles at its heart.

items.title: DRAG-Inspired Single Flux Quantum Control of Superconducting Qubits
items.summary:
Scalable control remains a major challenge for superconducting quantum processors due to the wiring, thermal load, and hardware complexity associated with conventional microwave-based architectures. A framework for qubit control based on Single Flux Quantum (SFQ) digital electronics is presented.

For transmon qubits, optimized control sequences are constructed from regular pulse trains framed by arbitrary subsequences (ramps), enabling DRAG-inspired leakage suppression in the discrete SFQ regime through genetic-algorithm optimization. For representative $Y_{π/2}$ gates, the resulting sequences achieve simulated coherent-control infidelities below $10^{-4}$, including leakage from the computational subspace.

The objective of the proposed approach is to demonstrate that coherent errors intrinsic to SFQ control can be reduced to a comparable level for a more scalable cryogenic control architecture. Memory requirements are reduced by storing only the optimized ramps, while a modular controller architecture supporting both regular and arbitrary pulse generation is proposed.

The logical complexity of this architecture is estimated from the Josephson-junction counts of its constituent SFQ cells. The proposed approach therefore combines low coherent-control error with reduced memory overhead and provides a basis for scalable cryogenic SFQ control architectures.

items.title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
items.summary:
Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32.

This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold.

We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

items.title: Qedma Appoints Scott Aaronson to Its Scientific Advisory Board
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Qedma has appointed Professor Scott Aaronson, a leading quantum computing and computational complexity researcher, to its Scientific Advisory Board.

Aaronson will advise the company as it develops quantum error suppression and mitigation software aimed at improving the accuracy of quantum computations.

His research on quantum computational complexity and the evaluation of quantum advantage aligns with Qedma ‘s work on assessing the capabilities of quantum hardware.

PRESS RELEASE — Qedma , a quantum computing software company specializing in quantum error suppression and mitigation, today announced that Professor Scott Aaronson, one of the world’s leading researchers in quantum computing and computational complexity theory, has joined its Scientific Advisory Board.

Aaronson is the Schlumberger Centennial Chair of Computer Science at The University of Texas at Austin and Director of its Quantum Information Center. Internationally recognized for his pioneering contributions to quantum computing theory, his research has helped establish the theoretical foundations for understanding the capabilities and limitations of quantum computers, including what it takes to demonstrate quantum advantage over classical computing. In 2026, Aaronson was elected to the U.S. National Academy of Sciences in recognition of his contributions to scientific research.

His appointment brings deep theoretical expertise to Qedma as the company works to overcome one of the most significant barriers to practical quantum computing: errors and noise that limit the accuracy and scale of quantum computations.

items.title: PsiQuantum and AMD Expand Partnership on Quantum Computing Infrastructure
items.summary:
Insider Brief

PsiQuantum and AMD have expanded their strategic partnership to co-design the classical and quantum computing infrastructure required for utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum systems and hybrid applications.

The collaboration will extend beyond AMD Versal FPGAs to include Instinct GPUs, EPYC CPUs and the ROCm software stack, alongside PsiQuantum ’s silicon photonics platform, with AMD also planning an equity investment in PsiQuantum.

The companies will initially focus on pharmaceutical research and drug discovery, building on work involving GPU-based simulations of covalent inhibitors and a machine-learning decoder designed for real-time error correction.

PRESS RELEASE — PsiQuantum and AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced an expanded strategic partnership to co-design the computing infrastructure required to operate utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers and the hybrid applications that combine quantum, high-performance, and AI computing.

The collaboration builds on the companies’ existing work around AMD Versal FPGA technology—selected by PsiQuantum for the development of its fault-tolerant quantum computing platform—and expands it into a broader relationship spanning AMD Instinct GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, and the AMD ROCm software stack, combined with PsiQuantum’s silicon photonics platform and its fully integrated platform. As quantum systems scale toward practical use, PsiQuantum and AMD expect the integration of classical high-performance, AI, and photonic quantum computing technology to form the world’s most powerful hybrid computing fabric.

To reinforce its commitment to the partnership, AMD also plans to make an equity investment into PsiQuantum .

items.title: Improved Low-Cost Quantum Error Mitigation with Benchmarked-Noise Zero-Noise Extrapolation (bnZNE)
items.summary:
We theoretically extend and experimentally demonstrate benchmarked-noise zero-noise extrapolation (bnZNE), a simple and low-cost method for quantum error mitigation which aims to outperform the highly popular ZNE method for an equal total shot cost by improving the classical extrapolation step. We recently proposed bnZNE as a new error mitigation method (Harris et al., arXiv:2603.10224 (2026)) and showed that it can mitigate noise to the same order as standard ZNE under gate-wise depolarizing noise.

Here, we introduce randomized bnZNE which addresses the case of running multiple random circuits per noise level, allowing for the incorporation of noise-tailoring techniques like Pauli twirling and readout error mitigation, and test the method on the IBM and IQM hardware for a plethora of large-scale applications, observing bnZNE to consistently produce more accurate results than standard ZNE. Our approach enhances the extrapolation process to the zero-noise limit by using classically-simulable and structure-mirroring benchmark circuits, generated from the standard application circuit, to sensitively measure the effective error rate at each scaled noise level beyond simple integer values.

We give a new method for generating tailored benchmark circuits for the IQM superconducting devices and test them experimentally. Our results demonstrate that bnZNE presents a versatile alternative to ZNE which can enable more accurate results at utility scales with an equivalent cost.

items.title: Communication Supremacy of a Qubit in Holevo Frenkel Weiner Scenario
items.summary:
The prevailing wisdom asserts that in the Holevo Frenkel Weiner (HFW) framework of communication tasks, a qubit offers no advantage over a c bit unless additional quantum resources are supplied or the classical shared randomness (SR) is restricted. In contrast, we establish the supremacy of qubit communication in the HFW framework when additional quantum resources, such as entanglement or measurement incompatibility are not injected and SR is a free resource.

We consider a prepare-measure scenario where the sender, Alice, prepares six states subject to a specific cryptographic constraint, and the receiver, Bob, performs a three-outcome measurement. Such a constraint on preparation impacts the power of qubit communication quite differently than that of c-bit communication, ultimately giving rise to the quantum advantage.

We introduce a witness capable of distinguishing quantum strategies that lie beyond the set of possible classical strategies and demonstrate the optimal quantum advantage. {As an application, we demonstrate the generation of certified randomness without requiring any seed randomness, since Bob has no input.} We further analyse the robustness of the witness and show that the advantage persists in noisy situations, making it suitable for experimental realisation. Finally, we demonstrate that Bob's three outcome qubit positive operator valued-measure (POVMs) has a distinct capability of detecting coherence, which can be regarded as the non-classical feature responsible for showcasing the quantum advantage.

items.title: Quantum Elements Helps Rigetti Predict Quantum Hardware Behavior
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Rigetti Computing is using Quantum Elements ’ Constellation platform to simulate quantum processor behavior and assess how its systems will perform at scale.

Rigetti said three years of collaboration validated Constellation’s ability to predict single- and two-qubit gate performance on its 36-qubit and 108-qubit processors.

Constellation now supports Rigetti ’s quantum error correction pipeline by supplying inputs for noise models used to predict logical error rates.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Elements , developers of software that shortens the path to fault-tolerant quantum computing, announces that Rigetti Computing , a pioneer in full-stack quantum-classical computing, is leveraging Quantum Elements ’ Constellation platform to model quantum device behavior to better understand how systems will perform at scale.

Constellation gives quantum teams a development environment for running high-fidelity dynamic simulations. Physically accurate quantum digital twins running on classical computers enable teams to design, test, and analyze quantum systems before committing to hardware experiments. Constellation provides this capability by modeling the physical behavior of specific quantum processors.

“ Quantum Elements ’ Constellation platform has expanded our ability to model gate operations beyond few-qubit systems and understand the error channels that limit their performance,” said Dr. Subodh Kulkarni, CEO of Rigetti . “Through three years of collaboration, we have validated the platform’s ability to accurately predict single- and two-qubit gate performance on our 36-qubit and 108-qubit QPUs. Constellation is now part of our quantum error correction pipeline, providing inputs for the noise models we use to predict logical error rates.”

items.title: Reduced filtering using classical control hierarchy with linear optimality for continuous quantum error correction
items.summary:
Continuous quantum error correction promises reduced thresholds and hardware overhead compared to the digital paradigm, but its complex model estimation has greatly reduced its practicality. We recast this problem as a classical control-theoretic state hierarchy made of an exact bilinear reduced model, an exact conditional filter, and standard estimation and feedback design.

For any $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code whose generators are all continuously monitored and which is driven by a single Pauli recovery channel, we prove that the exact filter closes at dimension $3\cdot2^{\,n-k-1}$. This dimension is set by the syndrome space instead of the Hilbert space and is minimal within invariant-subspace filtering.

The reduced model exposes and corrects two failure mechanisms of the feedback loop. Strong monitoring damps the rotational partner through which the controller steers the stabilizer and injects back-action diffusion along the recovery path; lowering the measurement strength during correction raises the entanglement fidelity of partner-steering LQR control by $0.096$ in the three-qubit code with three monitored parities.

Linearizing at the codespace leaves the syndrome uncontrollable, so the controller can stall; a gain designed at a shifted operating point removes this degeneracy. In the limit of zero measurement during correction, we prove that a syndrome-only filter is exact at every recovery boundary.

The resulting committed-recovery controller needs only $2^{\,n-k}$ class probabilities and gives the highest entanglement fidelity compared among the methods tested in the literature, $0.947$ against $0.920$ for a measurement-based estimator protocol in the three-qubit bit-flip code, and $0.726$ vs at most $0.407$ for continuous controllers in the five-qubit perfect code.

items.title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
items.summary:
Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture.

MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability.

A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction.

Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers.

These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.

items.title: Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
Speculative decoding accelerates text generation with large language models by letting a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large verifier checks in a single forward pass. We introduce Olifant, a draft model built on a memory-based classifier.

It predicts the next token from a four-token window in under 0.3 ms on CPU, requiring no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. We measure throughput and energy under two verifier regimes on consumer hardware.

Without a KV cache, drafting is nearly free: a domain-matched Olifant model reaches 38.1% acceptance on EU legal text, delivering 2.43x throughput and 2.51x lower energy per token than the neural verifier model alone. With a KV-cached verifier, itself a ~10x energy saver, drafting costs matter: a TinyLlama draft model halves throughput and triples energy despite high acceptance, whereas Olifant still yields 1.25x throughput and the lowest energy in the study (93 J per 100 tokens, 14x below the uncached baseline).

We further show that KV caching decouples time from energy: verification of longer drafts raises power draw, shifting the energy-optimal draft length below the speed-optimal one. Speculative decoding is not dead in the age of fast verifiers, provided drafting is nearly free.

items.title: Beauty and charm jet identification with end-to-end training on a superconducting quantum processor
items.summary:
The identification of heavy-flavor jets, i.e. collimated streams of particles originating from the fragmentation of beauty and charm quarks produced in proton-proton collisions, represents one of the most challenging classification tasks in measurements at Large Hadron Collider experiments. In recent years, advanced machine learning techniques have been successfully employed to address this problem, while quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising alternative approach.

However, the high dimensionality of the problem, typically involving hundreds of observables, raises an open question: whether the current generation of quantum computers, characterized by limited qubit count, can effectively tackle such complex tasks. In this work, a variational quantum circuit for the classification of b- and c-jets at the LHCb experiment is implemented on a 5-qubit superconducting quantum computer manufactured by IQM and installed at the Politecnico di Torino.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a quantum algorithm for jet identification using simulated data from an LHC experiment in which all stages of the machine-learning workflow, including training and testing, are performed on real quantum hardware. The results demonstrate that the impact of hardware-induced quantum noise does not significantly degrade the performance.

A framework for the evaluation of the training time on the quantum hardware and for the circuit optimization is also proposed. These findings pave the way for future applications on larger quantum devices based on superconducting qubits, featuring a larger number of qubits enabling the encoding of information beyond the reach of classical simulation and providing a step toward investigating whether quantum advantage may eventually be achievable in high-energy physics classification tasks.

items.title: Qunova’s Hybrid Computing Method Matches Classical Benchmark for Iron-Sulfur Cluster
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Qunova Computing reported that its HI-VQE algorithm reached chemical accuracy in an 80-qubit simulation of an iron-sulfur cluster using an IBM quantum computer and RIKEN ’s Fugaku supercomputer.

The workflow’s extrapolated ground-state energy estimate agreed within chemical accuracy with a leading classical benchmark calculated using the Density Matrix Renormalization Group method.

In an intermediate calculation, HI-VQE used approximately 300 times fewer Fugaku node-hours than a previously published sample-based quantum diagonalization approach.

PRESS RELEASE — Qunova Computing , a world leader in quantum computations for advanced chemistry, today announces that it s HI-VQE algorithm has become the first quantum algorithm to reach chemical accuracy (a level of precision required for practical use) at 80 qubits. It did so while simulating the 4Fe-4S iron-sulfur cubane cluster in a quantum / classical super compute workflow using an IBM Quantum System Two quantum computer at RIKEN , along with RIKEN’s classical supercomputer Fugaku. This result represents the most accurate quantum computation of the molecule to date.

Qunova ’s extrapolation of the cluster’s ground-state energy, −327.2482 ± 0.0007 Hartree, is consistent within chemical accuracy regarding the leading classical reference calculated using the Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) method (−327.2471 Hartree).  This result is more accurate than the latest extrapolated Trimmed Configuration Interaction (TrimCI) results. This places a quantum-based approach on equal footing, in terms of accuracy, with the strongest classical methods available today for one of the most demanding problems in chemistry.

“ 4Fe-4S has long been a proving ground where only the very best classical methods could compete, and today a quantum algorithm has reached that standard,” said Kevin Rhee, CEO and founder of Qunova Computing . “Our ground-state energy estimate is within chemical accuracy with respect to the classical benchmark DMRG,  making HI-VQE the first quantum approach to achieve this type of result at this scale. We are also very encouraged that our method points to a slightly lower estimate of the groundstate energy estimate of the true ground state. Our next goal is to identify additional industrial use cases where HI-VQE consistently delivers better results than the best classical methods. We believe this result shows we are on the right path.”

items.title: Circuit-Level Analysis of Quantum Error Correction in Second-Generation Quantum Repeaters
items.summary:
We present a circuit-level simulation of second-generation quantum repeaters with stabilizer-based quantum error correction. We model a two-segment repeater link including encoding, syndrome extraction, decoding, and entanglement swapping, and compare the performance of the single-error-correcting Steane and five-qubit stabilizer codes under different noise scenarios.

To that extent, we consider noise sources with incoherent (depolarizing and dephasing) and coherent (systematic over-rotation) errors and incorporate them directly at the circuit level. While the Steane code outperforms the five-qubit code at coherent errors, the five-qubit code achieves higher end-to-end fidelities under incoherent noise in the low-noise regime when a large number of physical qubits is affected by it.

At higher noise regimes, employing no code turns out to be the best option. In mixed noise scenarios, we observe moderate cross-effects between the noise classes regarding the error correction performance.

We conclude that code selection in second-generation quantum repeaters must be adapted to the dominant physical noise mechanism and that circuit complexity and hardware-aware implementation options influence performance in coherent-error-dominated regimes, providing design insights for error correction in quantum repeaters.

items.title: Climate Temporal Temperature Prediction via an Adaptive Stacked Bidirectional Residual Mamba Network
items.summary:
Accurate temperatures forecasting relies on traditional meteorological parameters that are essential for monitoring weather informatics and guiding forecasting efforts. This study presents Deep DualMamba, a novel deep learning framework for temporal temperature prediction, built upon an enhanced variant of the recently proposed Mamba network.

Unlike conventional Transformer-based architectures, which dominate foundation models but suffer from computational inefficiencies on long sequences, Deep DualMamba leverages selective structured state space models (SSMs) to achieve both scalability and performance. We identify a core limitation of prior subquadratic-time models-namely, their inability to perform long-term and robust forecasting and introduce two key innovations.

First, we propose an adaptive bidirectional Mamba as encoders to learn complex and efficient features. Second, we develop a hardware-aware, parallel recurrent algorithm to compensate for the loss of convolutional efficiency, ensuring practical viability at scale.

Last, the Deep DualMamba's approximation ability and convergence is theoretical analyzed. These design choices culminate in a simplified, attention- and MLP-free neural architecture that exhibits linear complexity with sequence length and significantly improved inference throughput.

To demonstrate its applicability in climate informatics, we implement a full forecasting pipeline using historical meteorological data from UK monitoring stations.

items.title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction
items.summary:
Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires classical decoders that can keep up with syndrome data streams and supply correction information and logical measurement outcomes to the quantum control system. Meeting these requirements at scale requires high throughput while controlling the end-to-end latency from readout to usable correction.

In this paper, we organize decoding algorithms, execution strategies, and code constructions using common classifications and examine their performance and trade-offs under the reported evaluation conditions. We distinguish decoder-level hierarchy, where multiple decoding stages or resources cooperate to decode a single code, from code-level hierarchy, where the code construction itself introduces multiple decoding levels.

We first review single-code hierarchical decoders and their cascaded predecoding and windowed, streaming, and distributed implementations. We then study hierarchical and concatenated codes, focusing on how decoding is coordinated across code levels through hard decisions, soft reliability information, or syndrome information.

We also examine how qubit modalities shape decoding workloads and timing requirements, and review how different decoding platforms meet these requirements, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), and cryogenic platforms. By assessing design trade-offs, this paper clarifies connections across the literature and provides a shared foundation for QEC design exploration.

It also identifies gaps in performance reporting and system integration to guide future research toward practical quantum error correction.

items.title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
items.summary:
Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100).

This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe.

SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role.

On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

items.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
items.summary:
vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.

Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling.

Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT.

Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE).

DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that DeepSeek's DSpark paper described.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning: Optimizing 0.6B Dense Models on TPU v7 via vLLM
items.summary:
Co-designing RL for a Qwen3-0.6B dense policy on Google Cloud TPU v7 across vLLM, Tunix, MaxText, and Pallas, with a 107x end-to-end speedup from ~100 minutes to ~56 seconds per true-8K RL cycle.

Authors — ASA: Loki Chen, Yang Song, Hongye Xie, Ming Lei, Greg Rehm, Chongyang Bai, Dre Olgiati, Bob Kamma, Tej Choudhary, Hang Cui, Imed Zitouni, Hamed Firooz. Ranking AI Research: Mingfu Liang, Kavosh Asadi, Yufei Li, Frank Shyu, Parish Aggarwal, Senthil Manickavelu, Xi Liu, Luke Simon.

Generative reasoning is reshaping how ranking and decision systems work. Models like GR2 (Generative Reasoning Re-ranker) [ arXiv:2606.31984 ] have demonstrated that generative reasoning can meaningfully improve re-ranking quality. The next question is: for large-scale ranking and decision systems, how small can the policy model be without losing that generative reasoning capability?

A 0.6B dense student distilled from stronger teachers could serve with much lower latency and cost, enabling broader traffic coverage, faster model refreshes, and more RL experiments per day. That requires the whole training cycle to be fast, and model FLOPs are only one part of it. At 0.6B parameters, rollout generation, synchronization, and framework overhead take a growing share of wall-clock time.

Because a 0.6B model has far less matrix arithmetic per layer than frontier dense or MoE models, fixed system overheads (host dispatch, synchronization, and KV-cache lifecycle) shift the bottleneck from FLOPs to coordination.

items.title: The Noise Floor of a Quantization Comparison: Engine, restart, batch and kernel drift, measured against 8-bit and 4-bit effects in two decision models
items.summary:
A quantized model is usually judged by comparing it with its BF16 original, but that comparison changes more than the weights. It often changes the serving engine, it always runs on a different server instance, it may change how requests are batched, and on some stacks the library selects a different kernel depending only on which packages import. We measure each of these sources on the same 2,400 public decisions for two of Cloudflare's decision models, Clef-flash (9B) and Clef (27B), on an NVIDIA GB10, and state every quantization effect as the excess over them.

Sources that are not quantization move between 0 and 0.92% of decisions. llama.cpp restarts are bit-identical on every record for both models. vLLM restarts flip 0, 5 and 20 decisions at BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 on Clef-flash and 4, 0 and 22 on Clef; a third instance of Clef's quantized builds (exploratory) leaves FP8 at 0 and puts NVFP4 at 4 to 22, depending on which two instances are compared. An engine change at BF16 flips 6 to 16, a batch-size change 8 to 15, and the Gated DeltaNet kernel transformers selects unasked 10 to 14. Quantization inside one engine moves more: for Clef-flash and Clef, 0.88% and 1.04% at Q8_0, 2.12% and 1.62% at FP8, 5.79% and 3.50% at Q4_K_M, and 5.79% and 5.67% at NVFP4.

On both models, every 4-bit interval excludes every non-quantization source. Two of our five pre-registered predictions failed, and the same two fail when the tests are rerun on the 27B: FP8 is not inside restart noise, and changing engine moves fewer decisions than 8-bit quantization does. Accuracy hides most of this.

Over the full 31,275 public questions, Clef's Q4_K_M build moves accuracy by a net six questions (-0.02 points [-0.20, +0.16]) while 436 of its decisions get worse (exploratory), and NVFP4 costs Clef-flash 0.95 points and Clef 0.65. We release the code, quantization recipes, per-record outputs and the pre-registration.

items.title: Researchers Explore Quantum Inspired AI Repair
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Researchers from QDeep and ITMO University developed Tree-Ising, a method that repairs repetitive reasoning in small language models through targeted changes to their internal weights.

Running on conventional GPUs, the method achieved 55.1% accuracy on MATH-500 for one model and increased another model’s GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4% under specific test conditions.

The team executed an eight-variable repair subproblem on an IBM quantum processor as a proof of concept, without demonstrating a quantum advantage or a complete model repair on quantum hardware.

Researchers have developed a method that repairs repetitive reasoning in small language models by changing selected internal weights, with a separate quantum hardware experiment testing a possible route for future work.

The study, by Hadi Salloum of QDeep in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and Ammar Ali of ITMO University ’s Lab for Efficient AI and Data, introduces Tree-Ising, a system for turning model repairs into mathematical optimization problems. The researchers describe the method in a preprint posted to arXiv .

The main repairs ran on conventional graphics processors. One solver uses simulated bifurcation, a quantum-inspired computing method that runs on classical hardware. The quantum experiment addressed only a small part of a repair problem and did not demonstrate a quantum advantage.
